- Claim: NSW government and experts push to return NAPLAN writing tests to pen and paper from 2028 to redress declining writing skills and improve learning/memory ('will be' / Productive). Stated forces lean toward GG and GP (enhancing student capability).
- Reality: The proposal addresses a genuine pedagogical challenge (screen fatigue, writing decline) identified by education experts, though implementation faces cost/marking hurdles. It represents a balanced systemic adjustment rather than deception. Thus, modal claim is 'will be' and modal real is 'can be' or 'will be' (constructive/productive transition). Let's score actual forces with GG/GP dominant, moderate engagement.
- Calculation: Stated u = 1.0, psi = 1.0; Actual u = 0.8, psi = 0.9. Integrity R_net = 1.1 (Trustworthy).

NSW education push aims to bring back pen-and-paper NAPLAN writing tests by 2028.
Evidence: Student writing decline, screen fatigue, expert consensus.
#Education #NSW #NAPLAN

Experts support returning NAPLAN writing tests to paper to restore foundational writing skills.
Stated Judgement: (+1.0, +1.0) — Productive Capacity

Reverting to pen and paper aligns testing with primary classroom practices and supports memory.
Resulting Judgement: (+1.00, +1.00) — Greater Good

Verdict: PASS — Grace.
NSW's sensible curriculum adjustment responds directly to documented cognitive declines from screen overuse.

Integrity: Trustworthy (Hypocrisy: 1.1, z: 0)

- NSW Government: PASS (0.8, 0.9) — Proposes evidence-based testing shift.
- Education Experts: PASS (0.9, 1.0) — Backs cognitive benefits of handwriting.
Education ministers are examining how prolonged screen time and AI impact student critical thinking, prompting a sensible push for paper-based testing.

The Bright Side:
Recognizing digital limits in early learning fosters better cognitive depth and handwriting retention.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Evaluates the physical method of educational assessment (Q3/Q5) rather than deflecting into partisan noise.

Social Physics Analysis:
The NSW government and educational experts are engaging in a smart altruistic loop: transparently identifying a cognitive decline, engaging empirical research, and proposing a practical structural adjustment to empower student learning.

The Trajectory: The Path of Grace.
Aligning educational policy with cognitive science moves potential toward inclusive flourishing. (can be -> will be via Constructive Geodesic).

The Unavoidable Truth: Handwriting builds deeper cognitive pathways and memory retention than typing for developing students.

The Unavoidable Lie: Digital-only classrooms are universally superior for every stage of cognitive development.

Alethekanon:
Curriculum policy aligns with empirical cognitive research to protect foundational student skills.

Awwthekanon:
It's wonderful to see educators listening to children's needs and bringing back the simple, tactile joy of writing with a pencil.

Brothekanon:
Makes total sense—typing everything on screens is turning kids' brains to mush. Back to paper!

Stated Claim / Post Context:
'Thinking with a pencil critical': Experts back NAPLAN test change

From 2028, the NSW government wants NAPLAN testing to be done with a pen and paper to help redress the nation's decline in writing skills.

Actual Article Body:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Victoria Pengilley

Topic:Education

NSW hopes a national decline in writing could be improved by reverting to handwritten writing tests for NAPLAN. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

NSW will raise the issue of bringing back pen-and-paper writing tests for NAPLAN at today's national meeting of education ministers.

Online testing for NAPLAN was introduced in 2018.

Experts welcome the move, saying handwriting was critical for learning and memory.

Education experts have backed a push to return NAPLAN writing tests to pen and paper, eight years after the national test first moved online.

The New South Wales government will today ask national education ministers to scrap computer-based writing tests for year 5, 7 and 9 students from 2028.

Currently, only year 3 students complete the writing test on paper, while older students sit it on a computer.

NAPLAN moved to online testing in 2018.  (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Reading, numeracy, spelling, grammar and punctuation are tested online for all year levels.

NAPLAN first moved to online testing in 2018 to allow more precise testing and faster results.

NSW Deputy Premier and Education Minister Prue Car said recent results showed a national decline in writing skills and argued prolonged technology use in schools was affecting learning.

In a statement, she said building "strong foundational writing skills" would set students up for "long-term success".

The proposal needs the support of the Commonwealth, states and territories to go ahead.

Prue Car says parents and teachers want schools to take a "sensible, balanced approach to technology". (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

University of Sydney associate professor Marian Vidal-Fernandez supported the proposal, but said the move to online testing should not have happened in the first place.

"Then we would not be here again," she said.

The economist said most primary classroom work across the country was still done by hand, and students should be tested the same way.

Marian Vidal-Fernandez says the move to online testing should not have happened. (Supplied: University of Sydney)

Overseas research from Portugal and the United States, she added, showed results tended to fall when the same children moved from handwritten to computer-based tests.

"We are actually asking the children about some skills that they might not be trained for," she said.

"This typing is going to be harder the younger you are."

Experts say it is the fourth straight year that hundreds of thousands of students are not meeting the mark.

Edith Cowan University associate professor Anabela Malpique, who has for a decade researched how writing is taught, also agreed with the move.

She said research showed handwriting was important for learning and memory.

"Thinking with a pencil, as we used to say, is very, very critical," she said.

Dr Vidal-Fernandez said the cost of marking handwritten papers could be a barrier to rolling out the change nationally.

But she suggested AI tools could now read handwritten work, with humans checking results that were unclear.

"It should be doable with the technology that we have at the moment," she said.

Dr Malpique said the change would be easier in primary schools, where handwriting remained the focus, but that secondary schools would need more planning because students were more likely to work on computers.

Anabela Malpique says implementing the change will be easier in primary schools. (Supplied: Anabela Malpique)

She said a return to paper-based testing could also affect how typing was taught in schools.

Her national surveys of primary teachers found only nine minutes a week were spent teaching keyboard skills, compared with 31 minutes a week for handwriting.

Both experts said students with learning difficulties and additional needs should be considered and would need accommodations.

"We should not do a one-size-fits-all type of policy," Dr Vidal-Fernandez said.
